title: What not to put on the site for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: What to leave off a B2B SaaS site
excerpt: Cut the feature grid that has no job. Keep the product in use and a way to book a demo. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long performance of taste.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. The article is about showing the thing itself and leaving the extra faces off the page.
caption: Two clear views of the object beat a crowd of features. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a B2B SaaS site?
faqs.answer: Remove a feature grid whose tiles do not name a job or show a screen. The grid reassures the team and flattens the product for an operator. Attach a real capability to a screen, or let it go.

faqs.question: Does a shorter site still need several pages?
faqs.answer: Yes. Keep a homepage, a pricing page, one proof, an about page, and a contact path, each with its own job. Short means fewer repeated claims, not a single scrolling novel that says everything and nothing.

faqs.question: Can a polished site still be the wrong site?
faqs.answer: A refined palette and large type do not replace a job and a demo. If the first three sentences could introduce any company, rewrite them until they could only introduce this product. Specific language is the polish that matters.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
B2B SaaS company website mistakes are usually additions. An operator who already runs software does not need more modules. They need the product in use and a clear way to book a demo. A feature grid with no job reassures the team and confuses the buyer. Cut it. A shorter site that tells the truth will do more than a long site that performs taste.

Taste can remain in the type, the spacing, and the care of a real screen. It does not need a slogan, a carousel, or a second version of the homepage further down. If a block does not help this operator see the job or book the conversation, it is a candidate to remove this week.

## Cut the feature grid first

The grid is the mistake that feels most like work. Each tile took a meeting. The icons match. The adjectives were approved. On the page, the tiles have equal weight and no screen, so the operator cannot tell what the product does on a Tuesday.

Remove the grid from the homepage. If a capability matters, attach it to a job and show the screen where it happens. "The approver acts from the queue" can stay. "Powerful workflows" can go. You will feel the loss in the design file and not in the buyer's understanding. That feeling is a sign the grid was serving the team.

Do the same to grids that have disguised themselves. A row of industries with no difference in the product. A row of integrations as logos with no sentence about what moves. A row of values. These are feature grids in softer clothes. Keep one integration if it is the reason a specific buyer can use you, and say what syncs. Release the rest from the first screen.

Google's people-first content guidance is a useful test. Pages should help someone complete a task, from knowledge you have, without padding. A grid is padding that looks like information. The task on this site is to judge the product and book a demo. Content that does not serve that task can leave, even if it is well written.

## Cut claims you would not say on the call

Remove award lines you cannot source, growth figures you would not defend, and customer quotes you drafted for them. This buyer has sat through vendor calls. Borrowed glory makes the real screen less believable, which is a poor trade.

Remove "trusted by" logo walls when you cannot say what you did for those companies. A logo without a constraint is a sticker. If you have one true story, link it. If you have none yet, skip the wall. Empty space is more credible than a fence of brands.

Remove urgency you have not earned. Countdown timers, "only three seats," and banners about this month's close are retail habits. An operator buying software for a team can smell them. State the price shape and the demo. Let them decide on a human calendar.

Remove the origin myth from the homepage. It can live, short, on the about page, and only if it explains a constraint you still honor. On the first screen it delays the product. The product is the reason they came.

## Keep the product and the demo

After the cuts, the page should still do two things well. Show a real screen of the job. Offer a demo with a label that says demo. If a cut threatens either, you cut the wrong thing. Restore the screen or the button, and cut a different ornament.

Keep the limits. Who it is not for. What is not included. Limits are not clutter. They are how an operator trusts the rest. A shorter site can still say no. In fact it should, because the remaining sentences carry more weight.

Keep one path in the navigation that matches the demo button. Same words. Same destination. A short site with two names for one action is still confused. Consistency costs nothing and reads as care.

Keep the title and the first sentence in the buyer's language. The job, the person, the object. If the remaining headline is a mood, you did not finish the cut. You removed the furniture and left the slogan. Replace the slogan with the job. Then stop adding.

## A shorter site still has a shape

Short does not mean a single scrolling novel with no pages. Give the buyer a few destinations that match real questions. The homepage for the job and the demo. Pricing for the shape of the cost. One proof page for a constraint and a decision. An about page for who does the work. A contact path that promises the next hour.

That set is enough for an operator to decide. More pages are justified when they answer a different job, not when they restate the homepage. A blog can exist. It does not belong in the header ahead of pricing. A resources hub that collects undifferentiated posts is a maze. If you keep writing, link it from the footer until a piece is good enough to support a specific question.

Each remaining page should be able to stand if the others disappeared. The pricing page still shows included and excluded. The proof page still shows the decision. The contact page still says what happens after they reach out. A short site of strong pages beats a long site of teasers that all point at each other.

Nielsen Norman Group's note that people often read only about a quarter of the words on a page is the practical reason to stop. Extra sections are not a safety net. They are words the operator will not reach if the first screen failed, and noise around the screen if it succeeded. Write the quarter you want read. Delete the rest.

## How to decide what goes

Print the sitemap, or write it on one sheet. For each item, finish the sentence "An operator uses this to…" If you cannot finish it with a job, the item is a mistake or a piece of internal news. Cut it or move it out of the public nav.

Then open the homepage and cover everything below the first screen with your hand. If the visible part shows the product and the demo, the page has a spine. Uncover the next section only if it answers a question the first screen raised. Repeat until a section exists because someone liked the layout. That section goes.

Do this with a colleague who did not design the page, and give them permission to be rude about sacred blocks. The grid is often sacred. The manifesto is often sacred. Sacred is a warning. Ask what the buyer would lose if the block vanished. If the answer is "our tone," check whether the tone is already in the sentences you kept. It usually is.

When you are unsure, remove the block for a week on a staging site and read the page cold. If you do not miss it by the second reading, it was taste performing as content. Ship without it.

## What a long, tasteful site still gets wrong

A site can be beautiful and still be a mistake. Large type, a refined palette, generous space, and a headline that could sit on any company in the category. The operator does not buy the palette. They buy the job. Beauty that delays the screen is the same error as ugliness that hides it.

Motion can be part of the craft when it clarifies. A quiet transition that keeps context is fine. A sequence that makes them wait to see the product is a slower grid. Respect people who prefer less motion. The job should be fully available without it. A page that only makes sense as an animation has trapped the argument in a flourish.

Photography of empty architecture, however calm, is still a substitute for the product. One real screen will do more than a film of a corridor. If you have spent the budget on the corridor, do not spend the hero on it. The hero is the product.

Copy that sounds like a keynote is the same issue in type. Read the first three sentences aloud. If they could open a conference and still not name the job, rewrite them until they could not open anything except this product. Specific is the polish. The rest is costume.

## Review the site as a cut list

Use a pass you can repeat every quarter.

1. Remove any grid whose tiles do not name a job and show a screen.
2. Remove claims, logos, and timers you would not defend on a call.
3. Confirm the first screen still shows the product in use and a demo.
4. Confirm the header has one map, with the buyer's words.
5. Confirm pricing, proof, about, and contact each do their own job or are absent on purpose.
6. Read only the first screen on a phone. If it survives, stop adding.

Then sit with the shorter page. The discomfort is the team missing its slogans. The buyer will not miss them. They will book, or they will know why they did not, which is also a successful visit.

The same discipline changes shape for a different reader. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing will punish a slogan even faster than an operator punishes a grid. Read [what the homepage has to prove for a developer-tool company](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-developer-tool-company) when the buyer is the person who will use the tool in a terminal or an editor, not the person approving a seat.
